intro: After the positive forms of “to be” (lesson 1), learn how to say “not” and how to ask questions. You need these sentences when you meet people, check information or correct a mistake.
objectifs: Make the negative of “to be” with not, in the full form and the short forms.
Ask a yes / no question by changing the order of the subject and the verb (Are you…? Is she…?).
Give a correct short answer (Yes, I am. / No, she isn't.).
Ask questions with a question word + be (Where are you? What is it?).

texte: To make “to be” negative, just add “not” after the verb: I am not, she is not, they are not. You don't need “do” with “to be”.

When we speak, we use short forms. For is and are there are two short forms: join the subject and the verb (she's not, they're not) or join the verb and not (she isn't, they aren't). Both are correct and common. “'s not / 're not” makes the “not” a little stronger.
With “I”, there is only one short form: I'm not. “Amn't” is not standard English.
exemples: The only short form with I.
She isn't at home. / She's not at home.
We aren't from Paris. We're from Lille.

sections.titre: Yes / no questions: change the order
texte: To ask a question with the answer yes or no, put the verb before the subject: You are French → Are you French? You don't need “do”.
“You are ready?” with a rising voice is possible only to show surprise. The normal question is “Are you ready?”.
exemples: The subject can be a longer group of words.
Are the shops open on Sunday?
sections.note: Negative questions (Aren't you hungry? Isn't it beautiful?) show surprise or expect “yes”. With I, say “Aren't I?”: Aren't I right?

texte: In English, only “Yes” or “No” can sound unfriendly. Add a short answer: Yes / No + pronoun + verb. Use the same verb as in the question.

Important rule: never use a short form in a positive short answer. Say “Yes, I am”, “Yes, she is”, never “Yes, I'm” or “Yes, she's”. In negative answers, short forms are normal: No, I'm not. No, he isn't.

lignes: No, he isn't. / No, he's not.
No, it isn't. / No, it's not.
Yes, we are. / Yes, you are.
No, we aren't. / No, you aren't.
No, they aren't. / No, they're not.

sections.note: In the answer, use a pronoun, not the noun: Is your brother at home? — Yes, he is (not “Yes, my brother is”).

texte: For an open question, put the question word first, then the verb, then the subject: question word + am / is / are + subject? The main question words: what, where, who, how, how old, when, why.

When we speak, “is” is often short after the question word: What's, Where's, Who's, How's. In writing, don't shorten “are” in these questions (write “Where are you?”). You will study Wh- questions in more detail in lesson 29.
exemples: Where are you? — I'm at the station.
Who is that man? — He's my boss.

texte: Never mix “to be” and “do”: “Do you are…?” and “I don't be…” are wrong. With “to be”, change the order or add not. That's all.

Some ideas use a verb in English, not “be” + adjective. The most common one: “agree” is a verb, so say “I agree” and “Do you agree?”, never “I am agree” or “Are you agree?”. But “afraid” and “right” are adjectives, so they use be: Are you afraid? Are you right?
exemples: Are you agree? ✗ → Do you agree? ✓
“Agree” is a verb: it needs do in questions (lesson 6).
Is she right? — No, she isn't.

formule: Negative: subject + am / is / are + not · Question: (Wh-) + am / is / are + subject? · Answer: Yes, I am. / No, I'm not.
prononciation: “isn't” /ˈɪznt/ and “aren't” /ɑːnt/: the final t is light, sometimes almost silent before a consonant (She isn't here).
Yes / no question (Are you ready?): your voice goes up at the end. Wh- question (Where are you?): your voice goes down at the end.
In questions, “are” is weak: Are you /ə juː/ or /ɑː jə/ in fast speech. In a short answer (Yes, I am), the verb is strong and stressed: /æm/.
In negatives, stress “not” or “-n't” so people hear it: I'm NOT tired. She ISn't here.
“What's” /wɒts/, “Where's” /weəz/, “Who's” /huːz/: the s joins the next word (Where's_it?).
erreurs: No short form in a positive short answer.
With I, the only short form is I'm not.
No “do” with “to be”: change the order.
A normal question changes the order; it doesn't use only the voice.
“Agree” is a verb, not an adjective.
After the question word, the verb comes before the subject.
Is your brother at home? — Yes, my brother is.
Use a pronoun in short answers.

dialogue.contexte: Two colleagues talk on the phone before a meeting in Paris.
lignes: Hi, Pierre. Where are you? Are you at the office?
A Wh- question, then a yes / no question.
No, I'm not. I'm on the train. Am I late?
No, you aren't. The meeting is at ten. Is Lisa with you?
Yes, she is. But she isn't very well today.
Oh no. What's the problem? Is she ill?
No, she isn't ill. She's just tired.
Yes, they are. They're in my bag. See you soon!

mots: Are you sure? — Yes, I am.
The museum isn't open; it's closed.
Is the station far from here?
Is she ill? — No, she's just tired.
No, you aren't right. You're wrong.
not busy; also: costing no money

exercices.consigne: Write the sentence in the negative (short form).
items: She isn't at work. / She's not at work.
They aren't Canadian. / They're not Canadian.
It isn't cold today. / It's not cold today.
We aren't late. / We're not late.

exercices.consigne: Change the sentence into a question.
Give a short answer (yes or no, as shown).
items: No, it isn't. / No, it's not.
No, they aren't. / No, they're not.
No, you aren't. / No, you're not.

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Correct it.
Write a question with “to be” for each answer.
items: The station? It's on the left.
Where's the station? / Where is the station?
No, they aren't Belgian. They're Swiss.

exercices.consigne: Write three questions with “to be” for a new colleague. Then answer them for you, with short answers and one full sentence.
items: Are you from Brussels? — No, I'm not. I'm from Liège. Is your office on this floor? — Yes, it is. Are you busy today? — No, I'm not. I'm free this afternoon.

a_retenir: Negative: am / is / are + not → I'm not, she isn't (she's not), they aren't (they're not).
Yes / no question: change the order → Are you ready? Is it far? Never “do” with “to be”.
Short answer: Yes, I am / No, I'm not. No short form after Yes.
Open question: Wh- + be + subject → Where are you? What's your name?
“Agree” is a verb: I agree, Do you agree?
